Business plan text:

Bristlecone Pets
Bristlecone Pets Executive Summary
Overview
Bristlecone Pets is a subscription service that leverages data driven personalization to
deliver durable dog toys and grooming supplies that are actually matched to each individual
dog. We are a student founded company, organized as an LLC, and we have a live website, a
working prototype app, and our first paying customers. This document is our executive summary
for the business plan competition.
The Problem
Dog owners spend alot of money on toys and grooming products and most of the time they are
guessing. A toy that is labeled indestructible or heavy duty is often destroyed within days by
a strong chewer, while a gentle dog may be sold a hard toy it never uses. The same is true for
grooming, where brushes and tools are marketed by breed but a dogs real shedding can vary a
great deal even within the same breed, season, and diet. The result is that owners waste money,
products end up in the trash, and the dogs themselves sometimes swallow pieces of broken toys
which is a safety concern. In our own informal conversations with about forty dog owners on and
around our university campus, most told us they had thrown away at least one toy in under a
week, and many said they simply gave up and buy the cheapest option because nothing seems to
last. There is no good way for an owner to know in advance what will hold up for their specific
dog. This is the gap we are addressing.
The Solution
Bristlecone Pets uses the information that is already sitting in every owners phone, which is
photos. Our customers upload photos of their dogs worn toys and, for grooming, photos of their
dogs coat and the hair collected after brushing. Our software then analyzes the wear patterns,
such as how deep the damage is, where on the toy it is concentrated, and how quickly the toy
broke down, and combines this with shedding indicators to build a profile of each dog. From
this profile we select toys and grooming supplies from our supplier network that fit that dogs
chewing intensity, style, and coat needs, and we ship them in a monthly subscription box. Over
time the profile gets better as the customer uploads more photos and gives feedback on how long
each item lasted, creating a feedback loop that improves recommendations for that dog and for
every other dog with a similar profile. We think of this as a data flywheel, where more
subscribers means better models, which means better products, which means lower churn.
Market
The pet industry in the United States is large and growing, and dog ownership in particular
represents a major share of that spending. Our target customer is the engaged dog owner,
typically a millennial or Gen Z household, who treats their dog as a family member and is
comfortable with subscriptions and apps. We estimate there are tens of millions of such
households nationally, and if even a small percentage subscribed to a service like ours at a
modest monthly price the market would be substantial. Our initial focus is on owners of medium
and large dogs who are heavy chewers, since they feel the problem most acutely and spend the
most replacing toys. We plan to start locally near our university and in a handful of similar
college towns, and then expand through online channels. We have not yet done a rigorous bottom
up market sizing and that is something we want to improve with mentorship.
Business Model
Our revenue comes from monthly subscription fees. We currently offer two tiers, a toy plan and
a toy plus grooming plan, priced competitively with existing pet subscription boxes but
positioned as more cost effective because products last longer. We source products from
wholesale suppliers and a small number of private label manufacturers and earn a margin on each
box after product cost, shipping, and packaging. Our early estimate of gross margin is in the

range of thirty five to forty five percent though this will depend on volume and supplier
terms. Longer term we see additional revenue from selling anonymized insights to product makers
who want to know how their products perform in the real world, and from a premium tier with
advanced tracking. Customer acquisition is currently through word of mouth, campus groups, and
local dog parks, and we expect to add social media and referral incentives. Our customer
acquisition cost at scale is still unknown.
Competition
There are several existing pet subscription boxes that send curated toys and treats each month,
and there are also large online retailers and big box stores that sell the same products one at
a time. Most subscription boxes personalize only by dog size or by a short questionnaire, and
none that we are aware of use actual wear evidence from the dogs own toys. Our differentiation
is therefore the data and the personalization, along with the focus on durability. We recognize
that competitors have larger audiences, bigger budgets, and established supplier relationships,
and that a larger player could attempt to copy our approach if it proves valuable. Our defense
is the proprietary dataset we build and the quality of our recommendations, but we acknowledge
that this advantage is early and not yet proven at scale.
Team
Marisol Teague-Okonkwo is our chief executive and leads strategy, partnerships, and customer
relationships. She has owned dogs her whole life and was the original source of the idea after
a frustrating run of destroyed toys. Declan Hrubik is our chief technology officer and built
the prototype app and the image analysis pipeline. He has studied computer science and has
experience with machine learning coursework and side projects. Priyanka Vandersloot leads
operations and finance, including supplier sourcing, fulfillment, and budgeting. All three of
us are students at our university and are working on Bristlecone Pets alongside classes. We do
not yet have an advisor with deep experience in the pet industry or in subscription retail,
which we see as a gap.
Milestones and Financials
To date we have defined the core concept, built a working prototype, and formed the LLC. We
launched a website and brought on our first external users, who tested the app and gave us
feedback on the photo upload flow. Our first client has paid for a subscription box, which
validated that at least some people will pay for the service. We have a small number of
subscribers right now and we are still learning about retention. Our spending so far has been
modest and has come from personal savings of the founders, covering the LLC formation, the
website, early inventory, and cloud costs. We have not raised outside money. Our rough
projection is to reach a few hundred subscribers within the next twelve months, which would
produce recurring revenue that begins to cover our costs, although our detailed financial model
is still being refined and several assumptions, particularly churn and shipping costs, are
estimates.
What We Are Asking For
We are asking for funding to help us scale from our early users to a larger subscriber base,
primarily to purchase inventory in larger quantities, improve our image analysis models with
more training data, and run initial marketing tests. Beyond money, we are seeking mentorship
from people with experience in consumer subscription businesses and the pet industry,
introductions to suppliers and potential partners, and feedback on our market sizing, pricing,
and financial model. We believe the competition would help us turn a promising early stage idea
into a real and sustainable business, and we thank the judges for their time and consideration.

Question: Comment on the viability and scalability of the business model and strategy. Address whether the company has a clear path to making money and growing, and evaluate the validity of the entrepreneur's assumptions.

response.text:
**Viability and Scalability of Business Model and Strategy:**

**1. Revenue Model:**
- **Subscription-based model** is viable and scalable, especially in the pet industry, where recurring revenue is common. The dual-tier pricing (toy vs. toy + grooming) allows for tiered monetization and caters to different customer segments.
- **Gross margin estimates (35–45%)** are reasonable for a subscription box model, but the company lacks detailed financial modeling, including accurate churn rates and shipping cost projections. This is a critical gap that needs to be addressed for scalability.

**2. Scalability:**
- The **data flywheel** concept (improving recommendations through user feedback and photo analysis) is a strong differentiator and supports long-term scalability. However, the **current dataset is limited** to early users, and the model's effectiveness at scale is unproven.
- **Subscription growth** is expected to be driven by word of mouth, social media, and referrals, which are common in the pet and subscription space. However, the lack of a defined customer acquisition strategy and CAC estimates raises concerns about scalability without external funding.

**3. Market Validation:**
- The **problem statement is well-defined** and resonates with pet owners, particularly those with heavy chewers. The **initial customer validation** (first paying customer) is a positive sign, but the company has not yet conducted a rigorous market sizing analysis, which is essential for long-term planning.
- The **target market (millennial/Gen Z pet owners)** is large and growing, but the company needs to better quantify its addressable market and customer acquisition cost (CAC) to justify scaling.

**4. Competitive Differentiation:**
- The **use of real wear data** from the dog's own toys is a unique value proposition, but the company must **differentiate itself clearly** from competitors with larger brand recognition and established supply chains. The **proprietary dataset** is a potential moat, but it is still in early stages and not yet proven at scale.

**5. Entrepreneurial Assumptions:**
- **Assumption 1:** That the **data-driven personalization** will lead to higher customer retention and lower churn. This is plausible but untested at scale.
- **Assumption 2:** That **anonymized insights** will be valuable to product makers. This is a promising long-term revenue stream, but it is speculative without market validation.
- **Assumption 3:** That **early users will scale organically** through referrals and social media. This is a common path for startups, but the company needs a more concrete strategy to accelerate growth.

**Conclusion:**
The business model has **potential for scalability** and **viability**, particularly if the data-driven personalization proves effective in improving customer retention and product durability. However, the company lacks **detailed financial modeling**, **market validation**, and **proven scalability**. The entrepreneurs' assumptions are **plausible but untested**, and the business needs **mentorship, market research, and a more robust financial plan** to move from early-stage validation to sustainable growth.
